name: Granby Roll Escape
description: Master the Granby Roll Escape from Aoki Lock in BJJ. Inverted rolling escape technique with 65% success rate at advanced level. Complete guide with step-by-step execution.
overview:
The Granby Roll Escape is an inverted rolling technique specifically designed to escape the dangerous Aoki Lock position by using shoulder rotation and hip movement to extract your trapped arm while simultaneously creating distance from your opponent. Named after the wrestling maneuver popularized at Granby High School, this escape leverages the principle of moving with pressure rather than against it, using rotational momentum to create space where direct resistance would fail.

This technique becomes essential when caught in the Aoki Lock because traditional escape methods that involve pulling the arm directly out or bridging away often increase shoulder torque and injury risk. The Granby Roll instead uses an inverted rolling motion toward the trapped arm, following the path of least resistance while your opponent's leg entanglement momentarily loosens during the rotational transition. The timing window is narrow but reliable when executed with proper mechanics.

Strategically, the Granby Roll Escape should be initiated before your opponent fully consolidates hip pressure on your shoulder. Once pressure reaches dangerous levels, the safer option is to tap rather than force an escape. The technique requires moderate flexibility and comfort with inverted positions, making it more suitable for practitioners who have developed basic inversion skills through guard play or wrestling backgrounds.
key_principles: Move with the pressure direction rather than against it - roll toward your trapped arm, not away from it
Initiate the roll from your shoulders and hips simultaneously to create unified rotational momentum
Keep your chin tucked throughout the roll to protect your neck and maintain body alignment
Time the escape when opponent adjusts position or before they fully consolidate hip pressure
Use your free arm to post and control the direction of the roll, not to push opponent away
Extract your trapped arm during the rotation when leg entanglement naturally loosens
Establish guard immediately upon completing the roll - do not pause in vulnerable positions
setup_requirements: Opponent has Aoki Lock control but has not yet applied maximum shoulder pressure
Your shoulder retains some internal rotation capability without extreme pain
You have space to initiate shoulder rotation without being completely flattened
Your free arm is available for posting and controlling roll direction
You possess adequate neck mobility and inversion comfort for the rolling motion
Opponent's leg entanglement is tight but not completely immobilizing your upper arm

execution_steps.description: Before initiating escape, confirm your shoulder is not under extreme pressure that could cause injury during the roll. If pain is sharp or significant, tap immediately rather than risking shoulder damage through the rotational movement.
Tuck your chin firmly to your chest to protect your neck during the inversion. Turn your head slightly toward your trapped arm side, preparing for the rolling direction that will follow.
Plant your free hand on the mat near your opposite shoulder, creating a pivot point for the roll. This arm will guide the direction and control the speed of your rotation throughout the escape.

Drive off your posted arm while simultaneously lifting your hips and rolling over your shoulder toward your trapped arm side. Your body should rotate in an inverted arc, with your back passing over your shoulder rather than rolling sideways.

As you rotate through the inverted position, your trapped arm naturally loosens from opponent's leg entanglement. Pull your elbow toward your hip while continuing the rotation to complete the extraction without fighting directly against their grip.

Finish the rotation facing your opponent with your newly freed arm establishing frames or grips. Immediately insert your feet between you and your opponent to establish open guard, preventing them from immediately re-attacking.

Once facing opponent, use both hands and feet to create active open guard control. Get your feet on their hips or establish hooks before they can close distance. Do not pause in transition - immediately create your defensive structure.

common_counters.counter: Opponent follows the roll and maintains back exposure
common_counters.your_response: If opponent follows your roll, continue the rotation fully rather than stopping midway. Complete the turn to face them or transition to turtle position where you have better defensive options than exposing your back.

common_counters.counter: Opponent tightens leg entanglement anticipating the roll
common_counters.your_response: Feint the roll first to make them commit to tightening, then execute a secondary escape such as the rolling escape to guard or address their base with your free hand before attempting the Granby.

common_counters.counter: Opponent drives hip pressure during your roll attempt
common_counters.your_response: Use their forward pressure momentum to accelerate your roll rather than fighting it. The additional energy they provide can actually make the escape more effective if you time it correctly.

common_counters.counter: Opponent releases shoulder lock and takes back control
common_counters.your_response: If they abandon the Aoki Lock for back control during your roll, you've achieved your primary goal of escaping the submission. Immediately address the back control with standard back escape sequences.

common_errors.error: Rolling away from the trapped arm instead of toward it
common_errors.consequence: Dramatically increases shoulder torque and can cause serious injury to the rotator cuff or labrum while making escape impossible
common_errors.correction: Always roll toward your trapped arm, following the direction that reduces shoulder stress rather than increasing it

common_errors.error: Attempting escape when shoulder pressure is already at dangerous levels
common_errors.consequence: Risk of significant shoulder injury including dislocation, rotator cuff tears, or labrum damage during the rotational movement
common_errors.correction: Tap early if pressure is severe. The Granby Roll requires initiating before maximum pressure is applied

common_errors.error: Lifting head during the roll instead of keeping chin tucked
common_errors.consequence: Exposes neck to potential injury and disrupts the rolling mechanics, often causing the escape to stall midway
common_errors.correction: Maintain chin-to-chest contact throughout the entire rotation, using your head position to guide the roll direction

common_errors.error: Stopping the roll midway in an inverted position
common_errors.consequence: Creates a worse position than the starting point, exposing your back while still having a trapped arm and no defensive structure
common_errors.correction: Commit fully to the roll once initiated. Either complete the rotation to guard or abort before starting

common_errors.error: Failing to immediately establish guard after completing the roll
common_errors.consequence: Opponent immediately re-attacks or passes your non-existent guard, negating the successful escape
common_errors.correction: Treat guard establishment as part of the escape - the technique is not complete until you have active defensive positioning

common_errors.error: Using arm strength to push opponent away instead of posting for the roll
common_errors.consequence: Wastes energy on ineffective pushing while eliminating the posting platform needed for rotational mechanics
common_errors.correction: Your free arm posts on the mat to facilitate the roll, not on your opponent to create space

training_progressions.description: Practice the inverted rolling motion without a partner, focusing on chin tuck, shoulder rotation, and smooth completion. Build comfort with the inversion and develop the muscle memory for the rolling arc.
Partner establishes Aoki Lock position with minimal pressure (10-20%). Practice the complete escape sequence including arm extraction and guard establishment. Focus on timing and direction.

Partner applies moderate pressure (40-50%) and actively adjusts position. Practice reading the timing windows for escape initiation and develop sensitivity to when the technique is viable versus when to tap.

Integrate the Granby Roll Escape into positional sparring from Aoki Lock scenarios. Practice combining with other escape options and develop the decision-making for when to use this escape versus alternatives.

variants_and_adaptations.description: Instead of completing the roll to face the opponent, finish in turtle position when opponent follows too closely. This variant prioritizes immediate escape over optimal guard establishment.
variants_and_adaptations.when_to_use: When opponent aggressively follows the roll and guard establishment is not immediately possible

variants_and_adaptations.description: During the roll, actively pummel your legs to establish butterfly hooks or de la riva as you complete the rotation. Creates immediate offensive guard rather than neutral open guard.
variants_and_adaptations.when_to_use: When you have superior hip mobility and want to immediately counterattack after escaping

variants_and_adaptations.description: Initiate the Granby Roll motion to cause opponent to react, then switch to a different escape such as the rolling escape to guard when they adjust their position to counter the Granby.
variants_and_adaptations.when_to_use: Against opponents who have successfully countered your Granby attempts previously

knowledge_assessment.question: What is the primary goal of Granby Roll Escape?
knowledge_assessment.answer: The primary goal is to escape the Aoki Lock shoulder submission by using inverted rotational momentum to extract your trapped arm while creating distance and establishing guard position. The technique prioritizes arm extraction through movement with pressure rather than against it.

knowledge_assessment.question: What position do you start Granby Roll Escape from?
knowledge_assessment.answer: This technique starts from Aoki Lock Bottom, where your opponent has established leg entanglement control over your shoulder and is applying or preparing to apply shoulder lock pressure. The escape must be initiated before maximum pressure is achieved.

knowledge_assessment.question: Why must you roll toward your trapped arm rather than away from it?
knowledge_assessment.answer: Rolling toward the trapped arm follows the path of least resistance and actually reduces shoulder torque during the escape. Rolling away dramatically increases rotational stress on the shoulder joint, potentially causing serious injury while making escape mechanically impossible.

knowledge_assessment.question: Your opponent tightens their leg entanglement as you begin the roll - how do you adjust?
knowledge_assessment.answer: Accelerate through the roll rather than stopping, using any forward pressure they provide as additional momentum. If they tighten before you initiate, feint the roll first to make them commit, then execute when they relax or adjust. Never pause midway through the rotation.

knowledge_assessment.question: When is the best time to attempt Granby Roll Escape?
knowledge_assessment.answer: The optimal timing window is after your opponent has established the Aoki Lock position but before they have fully consolidated hip pressure on your shoulder. If you wait until pressure is severe, the escape becomes dangerous. The technique works best when initiated during opponent's positional adjustments.

knowledge_assessment.question: What should your free arm be doing during the escape?
knowledge_assessment.answer: Your free arm posts on the mat near your opposite shoulder to create a pivot point that guides and controls the rolling direction. It should not push against your opponent - this wastes energy and eliminates the posting platform needed for proper rotational mechanics.

knowledge_assessment.question: What happens if your opponent follows your roll and takes your back?
knowledge_assessment.answer: If they abandon the Aoki Lock for back control during your roll, you have successfully escaped the shoulder lock submission. This is an acceptable outcome - immediately transition to standard back escape sequences from the new position.

knowledge_assessment.question: How do you know when to tap instead of attempting the Granby Roll Escape?
knowledge_assessment.answer: Tap immediately if you feel sharp pain in your shoulder, if your arm is fully extended with maximum pressure already applied, or if you cannot initiate shoulder rotation without significant discomfort. The Granby Roll requires some rotational freedom to execute safely - forcing it under extreme pressure risks serious injury.

knowledge_assessment.question: What is the critical action immediately after completing the roll?
knowledge_assessment.answer: Immediately establish open guard by inserting your feet between you and your opponent before they can close distance or re-attack. The escape is not complete until you have active defensive positioning - pausing after the roll negates the successful arm extraction.

knowledge_assessment.question: How does head position affect the Granby Roll mechanics?
knowledge_assessment.answer: Your chin must stay tucked to your chest throughout the roll to protect your neck and maintain proper rotational mechanics. Lifting your head disrupts the rolling arc and often causes the escape to stall in an exposed inverted position.

safety_considerations: The Granby Roll Escape carries inherent risk due to the shoulder manipulation involved in the Aoki Lock position. Never force this escape when your shoulder is under significant pressure - tap early if pain is sharp or rotation feels restricted. The rolling motion requires adequate neck mobility; practitioners with cervical spine issues should consult a medical professional before training this technique. Always maintain chin-to-chest position to protect your neck during inversion. Practice initially with cooperative partners at very low resistance to develop proper mechanics before adding intensity. If the escape stalls midway, do not pause in the inverted position - either complete the rotation or reset by tapping. The threshold for tapping should be lower when training this escape compared to competition, as repeated shoulder stress from failed attempts can cause cumulative damage.
position_integration: The Granby Roll Escape occupies a specific niche in the defensive hierarchy against the Aoki Lock. It serves as a moderate-risk, moderate-reward option between the safer rolling escape to guard (lower reward, lower risk) and more aggressive reversal attempts (higher reward, higher risk). The technique integrates with the broader inversion-based escape system that includes Granby rolls from turtle, front headlock, and various guard passing scenarios. Successful execution leads to open guard, from which all standard guard attacks and transitions become available. The escape also creates a decision tree for the opponent - they must choose between maintaining the submission and risking the escape, or abandoning the lock for back control. This dilemma creation is valuable even when the escape is not fully completed. Training this escape develops body awareness and inversion comfort that transfers to many other BJJ contexts.
